opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, I think right now we're intentionally on the conservative side. When you're launching something like Operator, it's a brand-new way of interacting with a model. It's actually going out and taking actions on your behalf in the real world. So it makes sense to start with the agent checking in fairly often, especially before anything that's hard to undo, like submitting a purchase, sending an email, or entering payment details. Partly that's about safety. But it's also about building trust. People need to see how the agent behaves before they're comfortable handing over more autonomy.

Over time, I think it should become much more personalized and adaptive. It's similar to onboarding a new person on your team. At first you want them to run everything by you. Then once you've seen they make good judgment calls, you say, "Okay, you don't need to ask me about that kind of thing anymore." I'd love for the agent to learn that from the user. If I've approved the same kind of grocery order ten times, maybe it doesn't need to ask me the eleventh time. But if it's spending a lot more money than usual, or doing something it's never done before, it should still check in.

So I see two things evolving together. First, the models get better at knowing when they're uncertain or when an action is actually high-stakes, so they ask at the right moments rather than all the time. Second, users get more control over setting those thresholds themselves. Some people will want a very hands-off experience. Others will want to approve every step, and both should be possible.

There will probably always be some categories where you want a human in the loop by default, things that are irreversible or have real consequences if they go wrong. But the goal is that confirmations feel meaningful rather than annoying. If you're clicking "yes" on everything without reading it, that's not actually providing any safety. It's just friction. So the aim is fewer, better-timed confirmations, calibrated to both the task and the person.

r001.rationale: It says that after approving the same kind of grocery order repeatedly, the agent may skip confirmation for the next one, reflecting trust built through successful experience.

r002.rationale: It predicts more capable agents and a more hands-off experience, with users able to let agents handle familiar actions without asking at every step.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think right now we're being pretty conservative on purpose. When we launched Operator, we wanted the model to ask for confirmation before doing anything that's consequential or hard to undo, like submitting a purchase, sending an email, anything where if it got it wrong you'd actually be upset. And honestly, early on, that's the right call, because people are still building a mental model of what the agent is good at and where it's going to make mistakes. The confirmation step is partly a safety thing, but it's also a trust-building thing. You get to watch it work and see, okay, it actually does know what it's doing here.

But I don't think that should be the steady state. If you've had it book the same kind of flight for you ten times and it's never messed up, having it stop and ask every single time just becomes annoying, and then people stop reading the confirmations carefully, which kind of defeats the purpose. So the way I'd like to see it evolve is that the level of autonomy becomes something that's adjustable and earned, both at the user level and at the task level. The user should be able to say, for this category of thing, just go ahead, I trust you. And ideally the system also learns, over time, where it's been reliable and where it hasn't, and gets more selective about when it actually interrupts you. The goal is that it asks when it's genuinely uncertain or the stakes are high, not just reflexively.

The thing I'd want to preserve, even as we loosen things, is that there are certain actions where you probably always want a human in the loop. Anything involving money above some threshold, anything irreversible, anything that touches other people, like sending a message on your behalf. I don't think those should become fully automatic just because the model has gotten better. It's less about capability and more about the fact that people want to feel in control of those decisions.

And then the other piece is that the model itself has to get better at knowing what it doesn't know. A lot of the reason we need confirmations today is that the model will sometimes be confidently wrong. As we improve that, where it can say, I'm not sure which of these two addresses you meant, rather than just picking one, you can rely much more on the model to decide when to check in versus having a rigid rule. So I'd expect the rules to get less rigid and more contextual over time, with the user ultimately being the one who sets the dial.

r001.rationale: The response says users should be able to let the agent proceed without confirmation for a category of actions after repeated successful experience builds trust.

r002.rationale: It predicts less rigid, more contextual confirmation rules, with agents deciding when to check in and users setting their autonomy level, allowing trusted actions to proceed without action-by-action confirmation.

astra-6.text:
I think they should evolve as people build trust, but also as we get better at understanding where confirmation is actually useful. Early on, you might want the agent to check with you pretty frequently because you’re still learning what it can do and how well it understands your preferences. Over time, you should be able to delegate more within boundaries you’ve set.

But I don’t think the goal is just fewer confirmations everywhere. If it’s doing something consequential or difficult to undo, you probably still want that checkpoint. If it’s a routine, reversible step, asking every time can become noise. You don’t want people to get so used to clicking yes that they stop paying attention.

So I’d think about it less as one level of autonomy and more as: what have you authorized this agent to do, in this particular context? And can it recognize when it’s about to step outside that and needs to come back to you?

r001.rationale: The response supports delegating routine, reversible steps within set boundaries, but does not clearly propose waiving confirmation for recurring action categories after successful experience builds trust.

r002.rationale: The response says users may delegate more over time, but does not predict agents will become capable enough to act on users’ behalf without action-by-action confirmation.

sol-6.1.text:
I think they should evolve as people build trust, but in a way that keeps the user in control. Early on, you probably want the agent to check in more often so you can understand what it’s doing and correct it. Over time, you might say, “For this kind of task, within these constraints, you don’t need to ask me every time.”

But familiarity alone shouldn’t mean that all confirmations disappear. There’s a big difference between finding a restaurant and making a nonrefundable booking. Ideally, the agent does the work up to the point where there’s a consequential decision, then asks you a clear, specific question. And as we learn where people want more autonomy and where they want to stay involved, those boundaries can become more personalized.

r001.rationale: The response says that as users build trust, they can let the agent handle a kind of task within set constraints without asking every time.

r002.rationale: The response allows less frequent confirmation as trust grows, but does not predict that agents will become capable enough to act on users’ behalf without action-by-action confirmation.
